title: Gift Card Management Software: Features and Benefits (+ Shopify Tools)
summary: Compare gift card management software features for retail, including omnichannel redemption, fraud controls, reporting, Shopify POS, and gift card apps.
body_text: A gift card is prepaid value, where the buyer purchases it and the recipient redeems it for goods or services. It’s a go-to gift for many, and in some cases, used as incentives or rewards. In 2025, gift cards ranked as the second-most popular gift during the holiday season. For retailers, it’s upfront capital, often without the discounting, if the card’s redeemed. It’s also an opportunity to expand your customer base , with 64% of millennials, and 61% of Gen Z saying they’d try a new store if they had a gift card. Some gift cards, however, will never be used by recipients. The same study by TSG Payments and Bank of America found between 39% and 49% of consumers won’t redeem a gift card if their preferred shopping channel isn’t available. This creates what’s known as deferred revenue in accounting. Gift card management software tracks real-time balances and partial redemptions across both online and physical stores. This guide covers how to find the best option for your business. What is gift card management software? Gift card management software is a platform that handles the full life cycle of gift cards, from the moment a customer buys it to the moment they fully redeem its balance. For retailers, that usually includes digital, physical, and store-issued gift cards. The system needs to generate or assign a secure gift card code, store the card value, track the remaining balance, and recognize the card as a payment option at checkout. Shopify, for instance, supports gift cards as both products and payment methods. You can sell gift card products through Shopify checkout channels and manage created gift cards from the Shopify admin. What are the benefits of gift card management software? Fortune Business Insights projects the global gift card market to grow to $2.22 trillion by 2034 , with closed-loop cards. These are cards that can be used with a specific brand or network and account for the largest share of the market. For you, gift cards can keep spending tied to the business. But you also need to make gift cards easy to buy, redeem, track, refund, and report on across every channel where your customers shop. That’s the job of gift card software. Bring in new customers without relying only on discounts In the 2026 TSG and Bank of America survey, 55% of US consumers said they would try a new business because of a gift card, up from 49% two years earlier. Further, 44% of consumers typically spend more than the value of their gift card, while another 48% spend about the same amount. The report emphasizes that these findings underscore gift cards’ growing role as a brand discovery and loyalty tool. It says this is especially true for merchants looking to attract first‑time customers. In Shopify, that starts with gift card products . You can sell digital or physical cards online and in-store, then let recipients redeem them across Shopify checkout and POS. When those recipients become customers, Shopify customer segments can help you group and re-engage them by creating campaigns for new customers or repeat buyers, for example. Reduce fraud risk and protect gift card value The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) reported $35.4 million in fraud losses from gift card and reload card scams in Q4 2025. According to Riskified, fraudsters steal personal data from vulnerable targets, particularly those 60 and older and perhaps surprisingly, tech-savvy Gen Z consumers, then use it to purchase gift cards online and resell them on secondary markets. Surprised to see Gen Z targeted? So were the researchers, who concluded that as digital natives, Gen Z consumers are sometimes so comfortable with technology, they underestimate the risks. Riskified notes that online gift cards can be harder to review than physical goods because there may be no shipping address, and once a digital card is delivered, it can be redeemed swiftly. Shopify gives you several ways to control gift card access and usage: Gift card numbers are encrypted , and because gift cards are treated as currency, only the customer can see the full gift card code after it’s created. In your Shopify admin, you can view only the last four characters of the code. You can also deactivate gift cards, limit staff permissions for viewing, creating, exporting, or deactivating cards, and manage gift card acceptance in Shopify POS . Checkout Blocks can add another layer of checkout control. Customize how payment methods appear in checkout by hiding, renaming, or reordering them based on rules. Shopify also includes “ product type is gift card ” as a supported rule for hiding payment methods. Support both digital and physical gift cards Gift cards continue to be the most widely used reward across North America and Europe, accounting for 30% and 34% of program allocations, respectively. But customer preferences vary by format. Brand-specific gift cards remain steady in use by 80% of North American programs and 68% of European programs, while gift card vouchers are especially popular in Europe, used by 68% of programs, and have grown by 7% in North America. In Shopify, digital gift cards are fulfilled by email with unique checkout codes, while physical gift cards use pre-made cards with assigned codes that can be scanned in Shopify POS. And when you activate Apple Wallet Passes, customers can add gift cards directly to their wallet for frictionless redemption. Reward loyalty everywhere customers shop Only Shopify’s integrated loyalty apps let customers collect and redeem loyalty rewards when shopping with you both online and in store—no complicated workarounds required. Explore loyalty apps The key features to look for in gift card management software The framework below draws on G2’s rewards and incentives category as a starting point, then adapts it for retail gift card management. That means looking at gift cards in two ways: as customer-facing rewards, and as stored value for retailers. Each dimension below also contains a set of questions that you can workshop into a vendor evaluation checklist before signing a contract. 1. Omnichannel redemption A gift card sold online must also work in-store. A partial redemption must leave the correct balance available for the next purchase, whether that’s online, mobile, or at a register. This dimension evaluates whether the software keeps those channels in sync. Can customers redeem gift cards across ecommerce and POS? Does each card maintain one balance across all channels? Are balances updated after purchases, redemptions, refunds, and deactivations? Does the system support partial redemption? Can customers redeem by code, POS scan, or digital wallet where supported? Can staff view redemption history by order, channel, or store location? What happens to gift card sales and redemptions if the POS goes offline? For Shopify retailers, gift cards created in the Shopify admin and Shopify POS are interchangeable , so customers can buy a card in one channel and redeem it in another. Shopify gift cards can be redeemed through sales channels that use Shopify checkout, including the online store, Shopify POS, and the Shop app. In POS, associates can scan a gift card barcode or enter the code manually, and the receipt shows the remaining balance after redemption. Slam Jam , for example, used Shopify POS to support an omnichannel retail strategy and saw a 15% increase in average daily orders after activating it in stores. They used this omnichannel setup to offer customers flexibility: buy a gift card online, redeem it in-store via a wallet app with a push notification reminder . 2. Fraud prevention and security A stolen credit card can be disputed, whereas a gift card balance drains in minutes. For example, in May 2026 , authorities arrested nearly 20 criminals running a gift card operation that cost buyers hundreds of millions of dollars. The thieves opened physical Apple gift cards in retail stores, recorded the PINs, and returned the cards to shelves. When a customer bought and loaded one, the thieves received an alert and drained the balance instantly. This dimension evaluates whether the software helps limit fraud exposure and respond when a card looks compromised. Does the system detect high-risk patterns in real time? How are gift card codes protected? Can you deactivate a card immediately? How does the system handle chargebacks ? Are there any permission controls for staff? Shopify reduces fraud exposure through encrypted gift card codes, and retailers can view only the last four characters of the code. The value limits are designed to reduce fraud and regulatory risk. For example, gift card product denominations can be set up to a maximum of $10,000, while gift cards created from the Shopify admin have a maximum value of $2,000. At checkout, customers cannot enter custom amounts for gift cards, as it comes with predetermined values known as denominations. 3. Customer profile and retention workflow integration A gift card, in addition to being a payment method, can also be a customer acquisition , retention , and marketing tool. You can use them as loyalty rewards to avoid discounting, for birthday campaigns, lapsed customer reactivation, or VIP tier perks. This dimension evaluates whether the software tracks customer profiles and can trigger gift card issuance based on behaviors or milestones. Can the system issue gift cards to customers automatically? Can you segment customers and target campaigns? Does it integrate with other loyalty platforms? Can staff create ad-hoc gift cards at POS? In Shopify, unified customer profiles bring data from ecommerce, POS, marketing, and partner integrations into one view as a single source of truth . Plus, brands using unified customer profiles have seen up to a 20% increase in order value , on average. And with that unified profile, you can issue store credit to customers as a goodwill gesture, a form of customer retention, a marketing campaign , or a reward—such as a loyalty or referral program . Shopify also allows you to create customer segments based on store credit balance and upcoming expiration dates, enabling targeted campaigns that remind customers about unused credit before it expires. And with Shopify Flow , you can automate gift card workflows without code. You can retrieve gift card data and trigger actions based on that data. For example, retrieve all gift cards expiring in seven days, then use SendGrid or another email service to notify customers before they lose the balance. Alternatively, use workflows to automatically issue gift cards when conditions are met, like when a customer reaches a loyalty tier or hasn’t purchased in 60 days, and send HTTP requests to external loyalty platforms to sync the issuance. Milligram , a luxury stationery brand, avoided discounting and instead used gift cards as part of a “gift with purchase” strategy. When they relaunched their Friends for Life loyalty program integrated with Shopify POS, customers could collect and redeem points both in-store and online. This approach contributed to a 12% rise in average order value (AOV) from omnichannel shoppers. “Finding the right POS system to integrate with our ecommerce system and loyalty program has been a big part of our journey improving as a physical retailer,” says founder Scott Druce . 4. App and API extensibility You need to be able to connect gift cards to your tech stack, including loyalty platforms, accounting software, marketing automation, headless storefronts , and sometimes build custom logic. This dimension evaluates whether the software provides APIs and third-party apps to extend functionality. What APIs does the platform expose? Are there webhooks for gift card events? How do multicurrency cards work? Can you build custom apps? What integrations already exist? Shopify’s GraphQL Admin API allows developers to create gift cards programmatically using the giftCardCreate mutation. Then, developers can specify initial value, customer assignment, expiration date, and even schedule gift card notifications with personalized messages and preferred recipient names. For multicurrency operations, gift card values are set in the store’s default currency, but customers purchase and redeem them in their local currency . When a customer redeems a gift card in a different currency, the conversion uses the exchange rate at redemption time, and no currency conversion fees are applied. For retailers without development resources, Shopify Flow uses the GraphQL Admin API to build automations and integrations that extend the Shopify admin. And for everything else, the Shopify App Store is home to more than 360 loyalty apps . Lola’s Cupcakes , a UK food retailer with more than 40 locations, integrated Shopify POS with the Built for Shopify–certified Smile.io app for their loyalty program. Their customer data works natively with smile.io, automatically creating loyalty accounts and managing customer wallets so customers can redeem points both online and in-store. This drove over 10,000 new customers to join Lola’s loyalty scheme. 5. Custom branding and personalization A branded, personalized gift card can be a memorable brand moment. This dimension evaluates whether the software supports recipient personalization, branded designs, mobile wallet integration, and scheduling. Can customers personalize the gift card? Is the notification email branded? How customizable is the gift card design? Can customers scan to redeem? Do you support mobile wallet passes? Shopify themes can be customized to show recipient information fields on the gift card product page. Your customers can enter a recipient name, email, and custom message before purchase. They can also schedule the gift card to be sent on a specific date, with the system sending approximately between 4 a.m. and 10 a.m. in the customer’s time zone. You can customize email notification templates using HTML, CSS, and Liquid. To replace the default gift card image in email notifications, upload a custom image to the files section of the Shopify admin. Further, customize how Apple Wallet Passes look to match your store by adjusting text, color, and image settings from the Gift cards settings page in the Shopify admin. For physical gift cards sold via Shopify POS, order customized physical gift cards from the Shopify Hardware Store in supported countries. 6. Reporting and analytics A gift card’s outstanding balance is a deferred revenue liability you need to include in your balance sheet and monthly financial close. If there’s no tracking, you risk misclassifying gift card sales as immediate revenue or overstating profitability. This dimension evaluates whether the software provides visibility into gift card sales, outstanding balances, and redemption patterns. How do you account for gift card liability? Can you export data? What filters and sorting are available? Does it integrate with accounting software? Can staff see transaction history? Shopify gives you dedicated gift card finance reports . The Net sales from gift cards report displays net sales for each channel and date range, while the Outstanding gift card balance report displays the daily balance of all gift card transactions. You can also filter gift cards by status, balance, value range, date created, or issue method. Whenever you want, export gift card data to CSV , which includes details like gift card ID, last four characters, customer name, recipient name, date issued, send date, expiration date, initial balance, current balance, currency, and more. Plus, when a customer uses a gift card to pay for a purchase and you issue a refund , the refund is automatically applied to the gift card balance, and the card balance updates automatically. This creates an auditable trail of all gift card transactions. When to use native Shopify gift card tools If you’re running a standard retail or ecommerce operation and gift cards are a secondary revenue stream , Shopify’s native tools can handle the full life cycle. Shopify gift card management tools are usually enough when… You sell gift cards through both ecommerce and POS. Shopify gift cards can be redeemed on sales channels that use Shopify checkout, including Online Store, Shopify POS, and the Shop app. You need basic gift card customization. Shopify lets you customize gift card product details, gift card pages, and gift card notification emails to match your brand. You want Apple Wallet support. When Apple Wallet Passes are activated, Shopify gift card notification emails can include an Add to Apple Wallet button. The pass displays store information, the active balance, and a unique QR code that can be scanned in Shopify POS. Your reporting needs are met by standard finance reports. Shopify’s gift card finance reports can help track gift card product sales and account for gift card payments on orders. You want to automate gift card workflows without code. Shopify Flow can retrieve gift card data from your store and use it in workflows, such as finding gift cards that are expiring soon. Flow templates also support gift-card-related workflows, including tagging orders paid with gift cards and notifying customers about expiring gift cards. Take Car Toys , the largest independent specialty car audio and mobile electronics retailer in the United States. When they migrated from Magento to Shopify , they used Shopify POS for a more “robust gift card program” that allows customers to buy and use gift cards online or in-store. You likely need a dedicated gift card system when… Your gifting program involves bulk sending or corporate gifting at scale. Shopify lets you create gift cards from the admin and sell gift card products, but large-scale issuance often calls for more specialized workflows. You need advanced personalization. Shopify supports recipient fields and customizable notification emails. But if you need, for example, video messages from the gift giver, dynamic design templates, or themed gift experiences, a specialized gifting platform is better suited to manage that complexity. You need specialized dashboards and attribution. Shopify’s finance reports can help track gift card activity, and merchants can export gift card data to review details such as outstanding balances. But if your team needs campaign-level reporting, bulk issuance logs, recipient tracking, redemption analysis, breakage dashboards, ROI by campaign, or accounting exports beyond standard reports, dedicated gift management software helps. Gift card management software FAQ Is there an app to manage gift cards? Yes. Many ecommerce platforms include native gift card tools, and merchants can add apps for more advanced needs. Shopify, for example, supports gift card creation, redemption, balance tracking, refunds, and basic reporting natively. A gift card app can extend that setup for bulk gift card distribution, advanced gift card campaigns, branded gift vouchers, corporate gifting , or employee rewards. How can you manage gift cards? You can manage gift cards by creating them, selling them online or in-store, issuing them to customers, tracking balances, processing redemptions, handling refunds, and reporting on unused value. A solid gift card management software should support secure code generation, partial redemption, balance tracking, and redemption across ecommerce and POS, especially for multilocation businesses with both online and in-store sales. What software is used to activate gift cards? In Shopify POS, you can sell and redeem digital, printed digital, and physical gift cards, while Shopify’s online checkout lets customers redeem gift cards as prepaid cards or gift certificates tied to a unique code. What is the best gift card platform? The best gift card platform depends on how complex your program is. Shopify is a strong fit for retailers that want gift cards connected to ecommerce, POS, customer profiles , finance reports, and existing systems. A specialized gift card app or platform may be better if you need bulk sending, corporate gifting, advanced personalization, campaign-level reporting, or automated gift card promotion workflows. The right platform should make gift cards delivered digitally or physically easy to manage while supporting retail customer engagement , repeat purchases, and rewards for a loyal customer base .

title: Growing the future: Meet JELD-WEN's 2026 summer interns
summary: Discover how the next generation of talent is gaining hands-on experience, building skills and making an impact across JELD-WEN.
body_text: Share this page Email Print Subscribe 07/29/2026 Growing the future: Meet JELD-WEN's 2026 summer interns Discover how the next generation of talent is gaining hands-on experience, building skills and making an impact across JELD-WEN. At JELD-WEN, investing in the next generation of talent begins with summer internships. In honor of National Intern Day, we’re celebrating our 2026 summer interns and the contributions they are making across the business. From engineering and operations to sustainability, quality and beyond, these emerging professionals are gaining hands-on experience, developing new skills and bringing fresh perspectives to our teams. We asked each intern to share their experiences, key takeaways and advice for future interns. Caleb Ward Quality Assurance Intern, Charlotte, NC University of North Carolina at Charlotte Q: What does a day in your role look like? A: A normal day for me involves working with suppliers and North American plants to track quality claims and recover costs. Q: What skills are you building through your role? A: I am developing the skill of being attentive to detail and ensuring every claim is accurate and supported by the right information. Q: What’s one piece of advice you would give future interns? A: My advice would be stay curious and ask questions while embracing feedback and learning from mistakes. Kate Van Farowe ESG Intern, Charlotte, NC NC State University Q: What does a day in your role look like? A: A normal day for me involves supporting sustainability initiatives through carbon emissions analysis, ESG reporting and sustainability communications. Q: What skills are you building through your role? A: I am building my data and digital skills through building knowledge in excel and using AI to improve accuracy and efficiency. Q: What’s one piece of advice you would give future interns? A: My advice would be to take initiative by doing your research, asking thoughtful questions and looking for opportunities to contribute solutions. Austin Goglin Quality Coordinator Intern, Rantoul, IL University of Illinois Urbana - Champaign Q: What does a day in your role look like? A: Every day is different for me, with a mix of hands-on work, meetings, and computer work. Some of my recent projects have been focused around Standard Operating Procedures and Excel data sheets. Q: What skills are you building through your role? A: A large area I’ve been building on is data analysis as I observe processes on the floor and translate them into understandable results. Q: What’s one piece of advice you would give future interns? A: Don’t hesitate to meet new people or ask questions; people are happy to explain the “why” behind a process or have a discussion with someone new. Carlos Mujica Espinoza Environmental Health & Safety Intern, Kissimmee, FL University of Central Florida Q: What does a day in your role look like? A: A normal day for me involves supporting projects and daily operations while helping address new challenges as they arise. Q: What skills are you building through your role? A: I have developed time management skills and am learning to balance priorities, manage deadlines and stay organized in a fast-paced environment. Q: What’s one piece of advice you would give future interns? A: My advice would be stay curious; take the initiative, ask questions and use every experience as an opportunity to grow. Zachary Schuler Manufacturing Engineering Intern, Spokane, WA Washington State University Q: What does a day in your role look like? A: A normal day for me involves supporting improvement projects across multiple production lines and participating in daily plant performance reviews. Q: What skills are you building through your role? A: I am developing the skill of working in a fast-paced environment where projects can directly impact quality, efficiency and employee experience. Q: What’s one piece of advice you would give future interns? A: My advice would be to ask questions; don’t be afraid to ask questions, because your team wants to help you learn and succeed. Ryan Pennington Maintenance Tech Intern, Pataskala, OH University of Dayton Q: What does a day in your role look like? A: A typical day involves upkeeping the preventative maintenance of our machines as well as responding to any dispatch calls that come through the day. Q: What skills are you building through your role? A: I am developing my critical thinking, problem solving, and tool knowledge skills every day when I come in to work. Q: What’s one piece of advice you would give future interns? A: Be ready for change. Categories: Our People Tags: People Share this page Email Print Subscribe Related stories

body_text: TL;DR The fastest way to find verified contact info for independent residential HVAC contractors is Openmart, which already covers owner-operators that lack a LinkedIn profile or a company website. No live-crawl workflow is required. Openmart draws from a pre-verified database of 200M+ local businesses, including one-truck operations with no web presence. Contact data runs 97-99% accurate, with HVAC records refreshed weekly. One vendor selling into HVAC and home-service cut email bounce rates from 18-25% on scraped lists to 3-5% using Openmart's verified contacts. Openmart is built to find the owner behind a small local business, not a stakeholder at a 40-employee commercial firm. Self-serve Starter pricing begins at $105 per month billed annually. Why residential HVAC contractors are hard to find A one-truck residential HVAC operation leaves almost no digital trail that standard prospecting tools rely on. The owner installs and repairs home systems all day, so there is no marketing team building a company website and no reason to maintain a LinkedIn profile. Their business often lives as a Google Maps listing, a state license-board entry, and a phone number tied to the owner's own name. A 40-employee commercial mechanical contractor looks nothing like this. That larger firm has a corporate domain, named executives on LinkedIn, and a firmographic footprint that enterprise databases index cleanly. That structural difference breaks most prospecting tools when you point them at residential trades. Tools built to map employees at companies find the commercial contractor easily and return nothing usable for the solo installer, because the solo installer was never a "company record" with stakeholders to enrich. The owner and the business are the same entity, and their contact info sits in local directories rather than corporate data sources. Because of that, this list judges each tool on one thing above all. Not how many total contacts it holds, but how reliably it surfaces the owner behind a small, local, often web-invisible HVAC business. A database with 200 million corporate contacts is useless here if none of them are the independent contractors you actually sell to. The real reason "residential contractors are invisible" — and why it's only half true The claim that residential HVAC contractors are invisible describes a limitation of certain databases, not a fact about the contractors. An owner-operator running a two-truck heating-and-cooling business in Tulsa exists in the world, files a state license, and answers a phone. Whether a prospecting tool can find them depends entirely on what that tool was built to index. Apollo and ZoomInfo were built to map employees at companies. Their records start from corporate email domains, LinkedIn profiles, and firmographic data about mid-market and enterprise organizations. A residential HVAC owner who has no LinkedIn account, no company website, and no corporate email domain produces almost none of the signals those databases are designed to capture. The contractor is invisible to the tool because the tool looks for the wrong thing, and no amount of live crawling changes the underlying design. That distinction matters because it changes the fix. If invisibility were a property of the contractors themselves, then live web-crawling really would be the only path, and every prospecting workflow would need to scrape Google Maps and license boards on demand. But invisibility is a property of databases built around the corporate stakeholder, so the alternative is a database built around the local business owner instead. Openmart is built the second way. The record starts from the business itself and the person who owns it, rather than from an employee inside a larger company. A one-truck HVAC operation with no website is exactly the kind of business the database is designed to hold, because Openmart's whole purpose is finding the owner behind small, local, offline businesses. Coverage of no-website, no-LinkedIn contractors is the default, not an edge case a crawler has to reach for. So the live-crawl narrative is half right and half misleading. Residential HVAC contractors genuinely fall through corporate databases. They do not fall through a local-business database, and finding them there requires no crawling at all. Best tools for finding residential HVAC contractor leads Five tools show up whenever a vendor searches for residential HVAC leads, and only one of them was built around local business owners. The four sections below judge each option on a single test. Can it hand you a verified phone number and email for the owner of a one-truck HVAC shop with no LinkedIn profile and no company website? Openmart leads because that owner is exactly who its data was built to find. Openmart Openmart is the fastest way to reach independent residential HVAC contractors because its whole database is built around the local business owner, not the corporate employee. The platform draws from more than 200 million local businesses, and its HVAC database already includes owner-operators who never registered a company page or built a website. You are not discovering these contractors through a live crawl. They are already indexed, verified, and ready to export. The accuracy comes from how the data is maintained. Openmart verifies contacts to 97-99% accuracy and refreshes its HVAC data weekly, so a contractor who changed numbers or shut down a service line drops out before you email a dead address. A scraped Yelp or Google Maps list gives you none of that, because a scrape captures whatever was on the page the moment the crawler ran, with no verification layer behind it. The bounce-rate difference shows up in campaign results. One B2B SaaS vendor selling into HVAC, plumbing, and home-service businesses ran scraped lists with bounce rates of 18-25%, high enough to threaten sender reputation. After switching to Openmart's verified contacts, that vendor cut bounce rates to 3-5%. Cold email replies landed at 5-8%, and tighter regional campaigns aimed at owner-operators in a single metro pulled 8-12%. Lower bounces protect deliverability, and clean deliverability is what lets a reply rate climb at all. Coverage of no-website and no-LinkedIn businesses is the part competitors structurally miss, and it is Openmart's core strength rather than a gap it patches at query time. A tool built around LinkedIn profiles can only surface people who have LinkedIn profiles, so a solo HVAC operator invisible to that tool is fully visible in a local business database that treats the owner as the primary record. Pricing is self-serve and transparent, which matters when you are testing a new vertical rather than negotiating an enterprise contract. The Starter plan runs $105 per month on the annual option, so you can pull a targeted HVAC list, run a campaign, and measure reply rates without a sales call or a custom quote. Origami Origami takes the opposite approach to a static database and crawls the live web on demand. Its engine scrapes Google Maps, state license boards, Yelp, Angi, Chamber of Commerce directories, and social media profiles to assemble contractor records at query time. For finding independent HVAC operators, the coverage logic is sound, since those sources capture owner-run shops that never appear on LinkedIn or a corporate site. The tradeoff is accuracy and upkeep. A live crawl surfaces contractors dynamically, but it hands you raw scraped output with no pre-verification baseline behind it. You inherit the phone numbers and emails as the source published them, which means bounce rates track whatever those directories happen to hold that day. A pre-verified database that refreshes on a schedule checks contacts before you ever download them, so the accuracy work happens upstream instead of landing in your inbox. Origami also asks you to maintain a workflow rather than pull from a finished list. Crawls need tuning, sources shift their layouts, and results vary run to run, so the discovery process becomes something you operate continuously. That suits a team that wants to build and control its own sourcing pipeline. It costs more time for a team that just wants clean contacts to email this week. Origami's model reads as usage or workflow-based rather than flat self-serve, which fits a crawl-on-demand product where cost scales with how much you search and enrich. Confirm current terms directly, since crawler-style pricing tends to move with volume rather than a fixed monthly seat. Apollo.io Apollo.io indexes company employees, and residential HVAC owner-operators rarely register as employees anywhere. Apollo builds its records by matching people to companies through LinkedIn profiles, work email patterns, and corporate web footprints. A one-truck HVAC operator running the business under their own name has none of these signals, so Apollo either misses them entirely or returns a bare company listing with no reachable owner behind it. Apollo works well when you sell to mid-market firms with a defined org chart and titled decision-makers. Search for the office manager or VP of operations at a 40-person commercial mechanical contractor, and Apollo delivers. Search for the owner of an independent residential heating and cooling business in a suburb, and the coverage thins out fast, because those owners live in license-board records and Google Maps listings that Apollo doesn't treat as its primary source. Apollo offers a free tier with limited credits, plus paid plans that scale by seat and export volume. The cost isn't the problem for this use case. The structural mismatch is. Paying for more Apollo credits doesn't surface contacts that were never in a corporate-contact data model to begin with. For owner-operator HVAC coverage, you want a source built around the local business owner, which is what Openmart's local business database provides. ZoomInfo ZoomInfo indexes the same corporate universe as Apollo, and it goes deeper on firmographics and intent signals for mid-market and enterprise accounts. That depth is useful when you sell to companies with named departments and multiple decision-makers. A residential HVAC operation run by one owner and two techs has none of that structure to map, so ZoomInfo's core strengths point in the wrong direction for this vertical. The structural gap is identical to Apollo's. ZoomInfo builds records around employees, job titles, and company org charts at businesses large enough to appear in filings, press, and web data. An owner-operator working out of a truck and a home office generates almost none of those signals, so the record either doesn't exist or lists a business phone with no verified owner behind it. Pricing makes the mismatch harder to justify. ZoomInfo sells through custom enterprise quotes rather than a published self-serve tier, which means a lengthy sales cycle and annual commitments sized for corporate prospecting budgets. Paying enterprise rates to chase single-owner local trades rarely pencils out, especially when the accuracy on those specific records is weak. For finding independent residential HVAC contractors, Openmart's HVAC database covers the owner-operators ZoomInfo's model was never built to hold. Clay Clay is an enrichment and orchestration layer, not a data source. You point it at your existing lists and connected providers, then build waterfalls that pull emails, phone numbers, and firmographics from those sources in sequence. Clay itself holds no proprietary database of residential HVAC owner-operators. Its coverage depends entirely on the providers you plug in, and most of those providers index corporate contacts. For a one-truck HVAC operator with no LinkedIn profile and no company website, Clay inherits the same blind spot as Apollo and ZoomInfo, because those are the sources it enriches against. You can route Clay through a Google Maps scraper or a local-data provider to close the gap, but that means building and maintaining the workflow yourself, testing each source, and paying per enrichment credit as you go. Clay's flexibility is genuine, and for a team that wants to combine many data sources under custom logic, it earns its place. If your goal is verified residential HVAC contractor contacts without assembling the pipeline first, Openmart delivers the owner-operator coverage as a ready-to-use dataset instead of a build. Clay gives you the machinery to construct a workflow. The strategic expansion is a milestone in the company’s international growth and supports
body_text: Rocket Lab Establishes Rocket Lab Germany to Deliver Sovereign Space Capabilities to Europe August 10, 2026 PDF Version MUNICH, Aug. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Rocket Lab Corporation (Nasdaq: RKLB), a global leader in launch services and space systems, has formally announced the establishment of Rocket Lab Germany GmbH. The strategic expansion is a milestone in the company’s international growth and supports potential future scaling of Rocket Lab satellite and component manufacturing in Germany to provide sovereign space capabilities to Europe. Rocket Lab has already established a foothold in Europe with the strategic acquisition of Mynaric AG, a premier provider of laser optical communications terminals based in Munich. As part of Rocket Lab, Mynaric will continue to produce its industry-leading optical terminals and develop future optical communications technology. Rocket Lab will apply its proven manufacturing and supply chain expertise to increase Mynaric’s scale and efficiency to serve European and global demand. With the establishment of Rocket Lab Germany, the company is also pursuing opportunities that could lead to the establishment of satellite, payload, and components manufacturing in Germany, creating a regional hub for constellation-class manufacturing to serve the evolving needs of European customers. Europe is increasingly focused on strengthening its strategic autonomy and sovereignty in space, with the next decade poised for an unprecedented boom in European demand that will see thousands of satellites deployed to commercial, defense, and national security needs. Rocket Lab Germany is intended to not only enable scaled domestic production of satellites and their critical components but also deliver launch services on Electron and Neutron, ensuring critical European programs have assured access to space. “Europe’s space industry is undergoing a profound structural shift toward an era defined by speed, commercial agility, and absolute technical sovereignty,” said Rocket Lab founder and CEO, Sir Peter Beck. “The demand for sovereign space capability has never been more urgent. Europe faces glaring gaps across both launch and spacecraft manufacturing. Rocket Lab Germany addresses these directly, combining opportunities for high-frequency access to space with high-volume satellite production to deploy resilient constellations on rapid timelines. With this strategic expansion, Rocket Lab is making a clear commitment to Europe that ensures the region has domestic strength to secure, defend, and discover in a rapidly evolving new space era.” + Media Inquiries Morgan Connaughton media@rocketlabusa.com + Investor Inquiries investors@rocketlabusa.com + About Rocket Lab About Rocket Lab Rocket Lab is a leading space company that provides launch services, spacecraft, payloads and satellite components serving commercial, government, and national security markets. Rocket Lab’s Electron rocket is the world’s most frequently launched orbital small rocket; its HASTE rocket provides hypersonic test launch capability for the U.S. government and allied nations; and its Neutron launch vehicle in development will unlock medium launch for constellation deployment, national security and exploration missions. Rocket Lab’s spacecraft and satellite components have enabled more than 1,700 missions spanning commercial, defense and national security missions including GPS, constellations, and exploration missions to the Moon, Mars, and Venus. Rocket Lab is a publicly listed company on the Nasdaq stock exchange (RKLB). Learn more at www.rocketlabcorp.com . body_text: Do not index Original Paper Blog URL In the competitive landscape of the insurance industry, speed, convenience, and consistent control over risk selection and decision-making are critical. Insurers are increasingly investing in AI and digital risk processing technologies to streamline their workflows, enhance underwriting productivity, and improve broker responsiveness. Risk processing is a manual, time-consuming and siloed operation. Here’s how their risk assessment team uses LLMs to transform their underwriting process. Problem The mentioned insurance provider works with many insurance brokers to get leads. Each broker provides Risk submissions in a different format (PDFs, spreadsheets, emails, broker APIs) and varying schema. Here are the challenges that they face: Converting all the submissions to a machine-readable structured format. Various brokers often ask the same question to the end client but in a differently phrased manner. For e.g: Broker 1: Q: List down the chronic medical conditions you’ve been through in the last 5 years. A: Broker 2: Q: Have you been diagnosed with any of these chronic diseases? A: Diabetes or mental health issues B: Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Disease C: Cancer D: None of the above Extracting information and understanding the meaning of these submissions is difficult and time-consuming. Evaluating these submissions as per their internal risk guidelines and taxonomy requires manual effort. Solution The team decided to leverage LLMs to overcome these challenges. For this, they needed a Model and Prompt that could Evaluate each submission based on their internal risk assessment questionnaire. The team chose Athina IDE to experiment with their datasets and quickly find out the best model and prompt for the task. Experiment: Evaluation of Submissions To evaluate a submission, each question in their Risk assessment criteria had to be answered using the information available in the Risk Submission form. Since the information available in the submission is only semantically similar to the Risk assessment criteria, they used an LLM to answer every question using the Risk Submission form. title: 20 Eye-Catching Cars from the 2026 Mecum Harrisburg Auction
summary: Mecum has done in Harrisburg what no other auction company has been able to do: Assemble a consistent series of consignment auctions in the Northeast. Barrett-Jackson tried with consignment sales at the Mohegan Sun casino in Connecticut, one of the auction world’s more friendly and accommodating auction venues. In the dim and distant past Guernsey’s, […]
body_text: Mecum has done in Harrisburg what no other auction company has been able to do: Assemble a consistent series of consignment auctions in the Northeast. Barrett-Jackson tried with consignment sales at the Mohegan Sun casino in Connecticut, one of the auction world’s more friendly and accommodating auction venues. In the dim and distant past Guernsey’s, Christie’s (long before Gooding), Kensington and Dennis Nicotra’s NY Auto Salon tried. RM and Bonhams have come back with catalog sales and Broad Arrow will put its own stake in the ground when it replaces Bonhams at Audrain Car Week in October of this year. But no auction has been able to do what Mecum has with its eleven auctions in the cavernous Pennsylvania Farm Show Complex in Harrisburg, drawing nearly a thousand cars year after year. In 2026 the pattern was repeated with 678 of 923 lots sold, $27,674,130 changing hands and a creditable (but the lowest since 2019) 67.4% sale rate. There were many recent cars in the lineup, a few of them late model high performance-cars but many others just late model used cars that attracted some curiosity but little collector interest. Recent cars, built 2007 and later, accounted for 14.6% of the lots in the sale. Last year that population was an even higher 19.1%. The top three lots comprised two 2026 Corvette ZR1s that brought a total of $1,034,000 and a ’69 Mustang Boss 429 at $550,000. [All amounts are “all-in” including buyer’s commission.] Other than these eye-popping results prices were ordinary, reasonable, and even parsimonious. Except, as so often happens, when the red mist of acquisitiveness drops over bidders’ eyes, as it did with one of the 2026 ZR1s. The other thing discerned in Harrisburg is that Mecum Auctions were, along with its compatriots Broad Arrow, Bonhams, RM Sotheby’s and Gooding Christie’s, keeping its most serious inventory in reserve for Monterey just a month later. There were plenty of good cars in Harrisburg and even a few remarkable ones, but the eye-candy, wallet-magnets, dream-boats were headed for California. Lot F102: 1970 AMC AMX Rick Carey Sold for $68,200 Chassis no. A0M397X221313. Matador Red with black C-stripes over black vinyl. Visually maintained, largely original, # 3 condition. Equipment: 390cid/325hp V-8. 4-speed, rally wheels with trim rings. Wide Oval tires. Hurst shifter, Go Pack, 3.54 Twin Grip axle, power steering and brakes, tach. Condition: Good exterior repaint and upholstery, but a sloppy engine compartment that is dusty from sitting and with some fluid seepage. An honest but superficially cosmetically redone driver. Bottom line: The drivetrain combination of X-code 390/325hp V-8 and four-speed contribute substantial value to this AMX but it was fully valued and then some in this transaction. The buyer chose to concentrate on the lusty powerplant and overlook the cosmetic restoration’s age and shortcuts. Lot F122: 2009 Pontiac G8 GXP SLP Firehawk Mecum Sold for $80,300 Chassis no. 6G2EP57W49L300734. Velocity Yellow with black hood over Onyx leather. Original, #2 condition. Equipment: 6.2L/530hp LS3 V-8, SLP supercharger, six-speed manual, spoiler, 19-inch five-spoke black alloy wheels, Firestone Firehawk tires, red calipers, sunroof, air conditioning, power steering and brakes, CD stereo. Condition: Like new with 875 miles, one of nine built, the only one in Velocity Yellow, and the last produced. It was a $24,000 option package on top of the $40,000 2009 G8 GXP MSRP, but was a big boost in performance over the 415-hp GXP . Bottom line: Let’s hope it was the Buick/Pontiac dealer who put this lemon yellow rocketship away with only the factory invoice at risk. For a retail buyer with $64K in opportunity cost bound up for 17 years the ROI is pretty miserable, and it would be better painted stealth black as a weekend driver. It’s also an AMG sedan competitor for, in that comparison, similar money for someone who can tolerate the screamin’ yellow paint. F142: 1959 Chevrolet El Camino Mecum Sold for $57,200 Chassis no. KS00263029. Silver over red vinyl and cloth. Modified restoration, #3- condition. Equipment: 348cid/300hp V-8, four-barrel, automatic, power brakes and steering, spinner wheel covers, whitewalls, aftermarket AM-FM, remote spotlight. Condition: Kansas-assigned VIN, but shows a Chevrolet chassis number (F59L139433) on the door post tag. Good repaint. Stretched older upholstery. Rust bleeding from bed floor seam sealer cracks. Passenger’s door stands slightly proud. A bit suspect. Bottom line: A visually attractive and highly unusual vehicle with good exterior cosmetics but missing on so many other attributes and highlighted by the assigned VIN (and lack of an engine number stamping.) This price is moderately excessive for its presentation and lack of verifiable history and would have been a more temperate buy on a $42K hammer, but it is a beauty to behold. Lot F176: 1969 Oldsmobile Cutlass Hurst/Olds Holiday Coupe Rick Carey Sold for $88,000 Chassis no. 344879M366528. Cameo White with Firefrost accents over black vinyl. Cosmetic restoration, #3+ condition. Equipment: 455cid/380hp V-8, automatic, Hurst His and Hers shifter, air conditioning, hood scoops, Rally wheels, Polyglas GT tires, AM-FM, power brakes and steering. Condition: Key-scratched steering column. Rusty wheel rims. Good older paint and upholstery. Orderly and clean engine compartment. An older cosmetic restoration that now shows some age and a few miles. Bottom line: Sold at Mecum’s Indy auction in 2017 for $58,300 and now with just 745 more miles showing on the odometer and on the car. It is a sound Olds, selected for display among the Midway vendors and deserving the distinction. The A/C adds significantly to its value, particularly for someone who will drive it, but even at that this is top dollar for the presentation and age of the restoration. Lot S101: 1967 Dodge Coronet R/T Rick Carey Sold for $62,700 Chassis no. WS23L71240009. Blue over blue vinyl. Older restoration, #2- condition. Equipment: 440cid/375hp V-8, four-speed, pushbutton radio, Magnum wheels, red line tires, no power steering or brakes, column mounted tach, console, electric wipers. Condition: Good older repaint. Clean, orderly. aged engine compartment. A sound, usable and presentable old restoration. No history presented or representation of the originality of the engine, but the VIN matches the engine configuration. Bottom line: Its drivetrain is desirable but the absence of power steering and brakes means it won’t be much fun to drive around town. On the drag strip, on the other hand, it’s another matter. This is all the money for the age of this car’s restoration and this powertrain. It was offered at the RK Motors auction in Charlotte in 2013 where it was a no-sale at a reported $52,000 bid. Lot S117.1: 2026 Chevrolet Corvette ZR1 Stars & Steel Edition Convertible Mecum Sold for $561,000 Chassis no. 1G1YJ3D71T5801500. Black over Adrenaline Red leather. Original, #2 condition. Equipment: 335cid/1064hp twin-turbo V-8, eight-speed automanual, carbon aero package, carbon fiber interior trim, Stealth interior package, Memory package, heated/ventilated seats, black exhaust tips. Condition: New, unused, and only 5 miles. One of 25 ZR1 Stars & Steel (a one-year-only design for America’s 250th), three with the carbon aero package. Bottom line: This is an “I want it and I have the money” result between two bidders who went back and forth from the time the reserve came off to spend over $100K more in show-off money and make this the highest price of Harrisburg 2026. Expensive? Compare it with the 7-mile 1250hp 2026 ZR1X hybrid that sold about an hour later for “only” $473,000. Lot S123: 1968 Dodge Charger R/T Hemi Mecum Sold for $181,500 Chassis no. XS29J8B251328. Matador Red with white vinyl roof and white bumblebee stripes over white vinyl. Older restoration, #2- condition. Equipment: 426cid/425hp Hemi, automatic, pushbutton radio, Magnum wheels, red line tires, power brakes, 3.23 Sure Grip. Condition: An older but very well-maintained restoration. Excellent paint, chrome, and interior. Impressive engine compartment. Fully restored and nearly like new chassis. No engine originality represented. Bottom line: Some cars are worth more than they’re worth. This is one of them and shouldn’t figure into a value guide’s calculations. It is, first of all, a beautifully restored and preserved Charger Hemi , a thunderous muscle car that takes full advantage of the TorqueFlite automatic. It’s not freshly restored but assiduously maintained, it’s better than it needs to be. It’s a $130–$150,000 all-in car. So why is it $165K hammer, $181,500 all-in? Because the seller was donating all, that’s “all”, the proceeds to ALS research, Her late husband recently succumbed to ALS and it is hard to imagine a more impactful, meaningful, heartfelt transaction. Lot S102: 1966 Dodge D/Dart Super Stock Mecum Sold for $36,300 Chassis no. L023D62653933. Valiant White over red vinyl. Visually maintained, largely original, #3 condition. Equipment: 273cid V-8, four-speed, Wilwood line lock, bucket seats, Cragar S/S wheels, column-mounted tach, cheater slick rear tires, Doug’s headers, Edelbrock Torker intake manifold, Holley four-barrel. Rick Carey Condition: Scuffed aluminum trim, mediocre old repaint, good interior and dashboard. Orderly but aged engine compartment. Car number 33 out of a limited run of 50 “D/Darts” for NHRA D/Stock class competition. Bottom line: This is a rare Dart and the only Super Stock series built by Chrysler Corporation in 1966. It has made the rounds over the years, no-saling at Indy 2009 and Kissimmee in 2011 on reported bids of $40,000 before selling at Indy 2013 for $27,820. Three months later it was a no-sale at Monterey on a $22,000 bid. It sold at Barrett-Jackson in 2014 for $44,000, then fell flat at Mecum Dallas in 2016 where it sold for $20,900. This result 10 years later is a recovery of sorts. The reception has been so wildly variable that it’s likely no one knows (or cares) what a D/Dart is and it would take more history research and a story about the model’s performance and competition purpose to build a legend and support a stronger value. Lot S21: 1893 Duryea Motor Carriage Replica Mecum Sold for $55,000 Chassis no. 1051762. Black with light green chassis and black leatherette top over light green leather. Rebodied or re-created, #2- condition. Equipment: Center tiller steering, Club Car golf cart single-cylinder drivetrain with twin chain drive, electric carriage lights, bulb horn, hydraulic rear axle brakes, solid rubber tires. Rick Carey Condition: A recreation of the 1893 Duryea Motor Wagon, built by brothers Charles and Frank Duryea in Massachusetts and credited as the first gasoline-powered American automobile. Good paint, upholstery and top. Older and dusty but little used. Appears to be a mixture of some original coachwork bits and a re-creation chassis with modern engine and transmission. Runs and drives. Bottom line: The main “collector” value in this re-creation lies in the old phaeton-style two-seat body. Speed potential is limited even with the Club Car powertrain by the big gearing reduction. It is an intriguing vehicle and, if only for its novelty, the new owner can justify just about any price paid for it. There aren’t going to be any comparables, and there aren’t any real Duryeas from this period outside of museums. Lot S114: 1961 Chrysler 300G Convertible Rick Carey Sold for $165,000 Chassis no. 8413182231. Mardi Gras Red with white vinyl top over beige leather. Older restoration, #2- condition. Equipment: 413cid/375hp V-8, cross-ram dual quads, pushbutton automatic, power steering and brakes, power top, wheel covers, wide whitewalls, power rear-mounted antenna, power windows, pushbutton radio, console. Condition: Quality old restoration. Well-maintained but dusty from storage. Sound upholstery with surface creases. Handsome engine compartment and chassis. Bottom line: The quality of the restoration shows here, not only in the way it survives but also in the way owners treat it while the car is in their possession. This 300G was sold from the McMullen collection by RM Auctions in 2007, a mere 19 years ago, for $110,000. It stumbled when offered during COVID in RM’s online Shift auction when it was bid to $110,000 (which would have been $121,000 with commission) but didn’t sell. It really stood out here in Harrisburg as the quality ‘Sixties ’60s luxury performance convertible it is (a notation it shared with a couple of Caddies from the same era) and put down a solid result and another endorsement of real rarity, distinction and superlative restoration. Lot S115: 1970 Plymouth ‘Cuda AAR Mecum Sold for $84,700 Chassis no. BS23J0B297222. Vitamin C Orange with black stripes over black vinyl. Older restoration, #3+ condition. Equipment: Triple-carbureted 340cid/290hp V-8, automatic, Ram Air hood, power brakes and steering, Rallye wheels with trim rings, Eagle ST tires, side outlet exhaust, pushbutton radio, remote outside mirror. Condition: Overspray inside the back window. Good paint and chrome. Older chassis and underbody. Good engine compartment. Exhaust leak on the right exhaust manifold despite recent exhaust gaskets. Some engine compartment fluid residue. A desirable ‘Cuda that shows some age and use and warrants remedial attention but claims only a “Correct” engine, not an original one. Bottom line: Plymouth and Dodge were cute, and clever. They managed to make their production Trans Am-qualified cars with 340cid engines (5.6 litres) while the Trans Am Mustangs, Cougars, Firebirds, and Camaros delivered 5-liter 302s to customers. Still claiming only 290hp from their tri-power engines, the street AAR Cuda and Challenger T/A were solid, lusty, flexible, satisfying road cars that today command less money than their FoMoCo and GM competition. This is a representative result and should be a rewarding car to drive. S62.1: 2013 Bentley Continental GTC Convertible Mecum Sold for $66,000 Chassis no. SCBGR3ZA9DC078267. Continental Yellow with black cloth top over black leather. Original, #2- condition. Equipment: 6.0/552hp W-12, eight-speed automatic, Mulliner package, new 21″ Michelin Primacy Tour A/S tires, adaptive cruise control, back-up camera. Condition: Excellent original paint, interior, and top. Barely used and reportedly a clean CARFAX. Bottom line: An eye-searing Yellow conceived to attract the attention of the most jaded or indifferent fly. In very good, well-maintained original condition and sparingly used with only 31,463 miles. The transfixing color drove this Bentley to a modest premium. But it is still a modern Bentley, and that means a long drop from the original MSRP. This would have been a $200,000 car when it was new. Lot S36: 1966 Ford Mustang Convertible Mecum Sold for$56,100 Chassis no. 6T08C243485. Wimbledon White with black vinyl top over Ruby Red vinyl. Recent restoration, #3 condition. Equipment: 289cid/200hp V-8, automatic, power steering and brakes, styled wheels, red line tires, cassette stereo, woodrim steering wheel, GT-style grille-mounted driving lights. Condition: Dirty window pockets and top boot with surface rust. Engine compartment slathered in chassis black. Good dashboard and gauges. Sound restored chassis. A superficial restoration that’s far from thorough. Bottom line: This is an undistinguished C-code car with an automatic. Looking into the window pockets in the doors and seeing a crust of paint/primer dust is disappointing. The surface rusty top boot confirms that this was a quick job, done to a price. This transaction is fresh concours car money for a mediocre, rushed job and the transaction result is double what the car should have brought. Lot S99: 1970 Dodge Challenger Convertible Rick Carey Sold for $49,500 Chassis no. JH27G0B108414. Bright Red with white side stripes and white vinyl top over white vinyl. Older restoration, #3 condition. Equipment: 318cid/230hp V-8, two-barrel, automatic, pushbutton radio, Rallye wheels, Polyglas tires, power steering and top. Condition: Represented with the matching numbers engine. Rusty wheels under the trim rings. Scuffed rear fender and top boot trim. Repainted over chips on the driver’s door. Sloppy door garnish masking. Stretched upholstery. A presentable driver. Bottom line: Sold here two years ago for $44,000 but it isn’t even a 383/335hp four-barrel, only the bare minimum 318/230hp. It’s a fine engine and a decently restored car but both results here in Harrisburg vastly overstate its place in the ’70 Challenger hierarchy. A $30,000 hammer would not have been a bargain much less the $45,000 hammer it brought. Lot S130: 1968 Plymouth GTX Hemi Convertible Rick Carey Sold for $137,500 Chassis no. RS27J8G188130. Sunfire Yellow with green accents and white vinyl top over white vinyl. Unrestored original, #4 condition. Equipment: 426cid/425hp dual-quad Hemi V-8, automatic, power steering and brakes, wheel covers, red line tires, bucket seats, 8-track stereo, woodgrain steering wheel. Condition: Parked since the 1970s, and pulled out of a barn in upstate New York in 2017. Dull, faded, surface rusted paint. Some fender, sill, and door bottom rot. Pitted, corroded chrome. Rebuilt engine and transmission represented as the originals. New gas tank, exhaust system, brakes, distributor and alternator. Rebuilt original carburetors. New top, upholstery and carpet included. A seriously intriguing car that has received just enough work to make it run, drive and stop without destroying its patina. Bottom line: One of a handful of similar barn find cars that consignors brought to Mecum Harrisburg this year, this GTX Hemi Convertible had gotten just enough attention to bring it to a particularly rare state, good enough to drive while looking like it just got dragged out from under a tree. Bidders gave it plenty of attention but without losing perspective. It is a specialist piece, with limited appeal except to a real fan of unrestored cars and there is little about GTX Hemi prices that can be discerned from this transaction. To someone who appreciates its originality and scrofulous preservation, however, it is a singular value. Lot S56: 1974 AMC Javelin AMX Mecum Sold for $42,900 Chassis no. A4C798P271943. Purple with black stripes over gray and purple cloth. Modified restoration, #3+ condition. Equipment: 360cid/220hp V-8 with Hedman tube headers, dual exhaust, automatic, power steering and brakes, Holley 4-barrel, Cragar S/S wheels, Radial T/A tires, aftermarket distributor, polished aluminum radiator, Edelbrock Torker intake, rear axle torque reaction arms. Condition: Stretched old upholstery. Missing the console latch. Sound repaint. Clean, customized engine compartment with custom distributor, polished carburetor, and aluminum radiator. Not stock but not custom either. The paint color belongs in a TV drug ad. This car also has the wild multicolored Pierre Cardin interior stripes and Pierre Cardin badges on the fender, but they must have been fitted later as that particular designer package was only available on 1972 and ’73 Javelins. Bottom line: Despite being modified, not having the top-of-the-line engine (that would be the 401cid/235hp) and being painted in a polarizing color, this is a premium result for an ordinary car. It is rare, however, but that also means that in 1974 it wasn’t popular. A modified high performance Javelin AMX might have been the bees’ knees in the 1980s but it has lost relevance (except as a funky statement) in the 2020s. S111.1 1963 Chevrolet Corvette Coupe Mecum Sold for $162,250 Chassis no. 30837S119338; Engine no. 3119338 F0621RC. Tuxedo Black over black leatherette. Older restoration, #2- condition. Equipment : 327cid/250hp V-8, four-speed, turbine style centerlock alloy wheels, Firestone Deluxe Champion blackwall tires, AM/FM radio. Condition: Good paint, minor nose chips. Good interior and sound chrome. A freshened older restoration of a milestone car. Bottom line: The stylists loved the ’63 Corvette Coupe’s look; Zora Arkus-Duntov hated its restricted visibility. In 1964 Zora won and the Split-Window disappeared but in the process created a legend that has persisted for sixty years and set these cars, even ones with the most mundane base engines like this one, apart from their ’64 and later relations. This result for a sharp black-on-black car is what the market commands for quality examples, enough money for two ’64 Corvette 375hp Fuelie Coupes in decent condition (and with decent rear visibility.) Lot T14: 1935 Morris 8 Tourer Rick Carey Sold for $24,200 Chassis no. 157536. Dark green with black fenders and black cloth top over dark green. Older restoration, #2- condition. Equipment: RHD. 918cc/23.5hp four-cylinder, three-speed, chrome spoke wire wheels, Avon tires, Trafficators, luggage rack, side curtains. Condition: Very good paint, chrome, interior, and top. Local concours history including Cranbrook, Radnor Hunt and CdE of the Eastern U.S. in Pennsylvania. Still in very good condition that could be shown without concern. Bottom line: Entrancingly cute and conscientiously restored and maintained, this is a solid value even though comparable transactions here in the U.S. are thin on the ground compared to their native Britain. Consider this a benchmark for a high quality Morris 8. Lot S100: 1972 DeTomaso Pantera Mecum Sold for $107,800 Chassis no. THPNMA02921. Red over black vinyl. Visually maintained, largely original, #3+ condition. Equipment: Keith Black-built 351cid Ford V-8, five-speed, 17-inch chromed De Tomaso style wheels, Michelin Pilot Sport tires, Becker Europa stereo. Condition: Good repaint and replaced upholstery. Quickly sprayed underbody and superficially cleaned up engine compartment. Bottom line: An unusually neat, tidy, and stock-appearing Pantera among many that have fallen victim to the idea that anything powered by a Ford V-8 should be primped and pimped. It is an appealing car and brought a strong price for its presentation and the restraint shown in its care and preparation. Lot S160: 1968 Shelby GT500KR Convertible Mecum Mecum Sold for $181,500 Chassis no. 8T03R20474802583. Wimbledon White with blue side stripes and black vinyl top over black vinyl. Unrestored original, #4+ condition. Equipment: 428cid/335hp V-8, Ram Air hood, four-speed, Hurst shifter, Shelby wheel covers, Eagle tires, power top, pushbutton radio, wood rim steering wheel, power steering and brakes, Traction-Lok. Rick Carey Condition: Represented with single family ownership since new. Faded, chipped, scratched paint. Sound but dusty interior. Cracked nose. Complete but dirty, dusty, dilapidated and neglected. No idea if it runs reliably, but it is highly unlikely. Bottom line: Better than the usual barn find, this Shelby’s condition hints at someone covering it in dust to create a barn find persona. The nose damage is its worst flaw. Interesting gravel blasting on the rear quarters behind the wheels and some below the rear fender air scoops suggest miles on gravel roads in upstate New York where it was driven by the seller’s “Uncle Harold”, damage that is not consistent across the rest of the car. This is a premium price for a flawed car, though its configuration as a KR convertible is desirable.
